title: Accidentals and key signatures
summary: How long accidentals last, key signatures in every clef, and enharmonic spellings.

provenance.notes: Items drawn from the seeded generators with a teaching-point filter, then fixed. Music and answers come from the rule engine; prompts and feedback are original.

items.prompt: What is the note marked *? Give its letter name and any sharp, flat or natural that applies to it.

music.textAlternative: treble clef, key signature: 1 sharp, 4/4. Bar 1: E 4th space with a sharp sign, E 4th space with a natural sign, D 4th line, E 4th space (marked *).

hints: Go through the bar from the beginning.
A bar-line cancels accidentals unless a tie crosses it.
An accidental lasts until the end of the bar, but only on its own line or space. A key signature applies in every octave.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed the accidental through the bar and stopped at the bar-line.

mistakes.accidental-forgotten: An accidental keeps working for the rest of the bar on that line or space.
mistakes.accidental-carried-over-barline: A bar-line cancels accidentals — unless the note is tied across it.
mistakes.key-signature-ignored: Don't forget the key signature: it affects every note with that letter name.
mistakes.different-octave-assumed: An accidental only affects notes on the same line or space — not the same letter in another octave.
mistakes.tie-over-barline: A tie carries the accidental into the next bar, but only for the tied note.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Go through the bar from the start, tracking each accidental.

items.prompt: Name the major key with this key signature.
hints: F♯ sits on the top line in treble and the fourth line in bass.
For sharps, the key is a semitone above the last sharp. For flats, it is the second-to-last flat (F major has one flat).

feedback.correct: Right. You read the key signature and named the key.

mistakes.wrong-count: Count again: each key has a fixed number of sharps or flats.
mistakes.wrong-order: Key signatures always follow the same order. Check which comes first.
mistakes.wrong-placement: The accidentals are right, but some are on the wrong line or space for this clef.
mistakes.relative-confusion: That key shares this key signature, but it's the relative key. Check the tonic.
mistakes.mixed-sharps-flats: A key signature uses only sharps or only flats.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Recall the order of sharps or flats and count how many the key needs.

items.prompt: Write the key signature of D minor in the bass clef.
hints: Recall the order of sharps or flats.
Sharps are written in the order F C G D A E B; flats in the order B E A D G C F.

feedback.correct: Well written: right accidentals, right order, right places for the bass clef.

mistakes.wrong-count: Count again: each key has a fixed number of sharps or flats.
mistakes.wrong-order: Key signatures always follow the same order. Check which comes first.
mistakes.wrong-placement: The accidentals are right, but some are on the wrong line or space for this clef.
mistakes.relative-confusion: That key shares this key signature, but it's the relative key. Check the tonic.
mistakes.mixed-sharps-flats: A key signature uses only sharps or only flats.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Recall the order of sharps or flats and count how many the key needs.

items.prompt: What is the relative major of D minor?
hints: Relative keys share a key signature. The relative minor starts on the 6th note of the major scale.

feedback.correct: Yes. Relative keys share a key signature.

mistakes.wrong-count: Count again: each key has a fixed number of sharps or flats.
mistakes.wrong-order: Key signatures always follow the same order. Check which comes first.
mistakes.wrong-placement: The accidentals are right, but some are on the wrong line or space for this clef.
mistakes.relative-confusion: That key shares this key signature, but it's the relative key. Check the tonic.
mistakes.mixed-sharps-flats: A key signature uses only sharps or only flats.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Recall the order of sharps or flats and count how many the key needs.

items.prompt: Give a note that sounds the same as E but has a different letter name.
hints: Find it on the keyboard first.
Find the key on the keyboard, then name it from the white key on either side.

feedback.correct: Yes. Same key on the piano, different letter name.

mistakes.same-spelling-given: The question asks for a different name for the same sound.
mistakes.not-same-pitch: That note sounds at a different pitch. An enharmonic equivalent must sound exactly the same.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Find the key on the keyboard, then list every name it can have.
